title: Six Columns
eyebrow: Your ruling on what a review is for, built and running

actions.fyi: Your ruling is in and all six columns are live on your board. Every call it left is below, each one overridable by its number.

content.label: What your board told you, and what it does now
content.lead: The thing you caught, and the four changes your ruling turned into.

rows.title: What you caught
rows.note: The fog job drawn under Agent Review with all forty-two pieces beneath it untouched. Two cards four levels down put it there, and the third column meant something else entirely: written, but not in the game yet. That is a landing, not a review, which is why an agent looked like it asked to be read after every small step.

rows.title: A piece of work has three places
rows.note: Waiting, being worked, done. Work that is written but not yet in the game leaves a piece being worked, because it is still in somebody's hands. Asking for a piece to be read is refused, and the refusal names the rule.

rows.title: A job is put in its column by its own pieces
rows.note: Picking one up moves the job to In Progress. It reaches Agent Review at the one moment nobody is building, and passes from there to your column. The three cards that were sitting in Agent Review as pieces have been put back where they belong.

rows.title: The screen reads one level and no deeper
rows.note: A card and the list of pieces printed under it can no longer say different things. Fourteen cases hold that line, including the exact shape you caught, and the fog job now draws under Todo where it belongs.

rows.title: All six columns are on your screen
rows.note: Read back off the running board by a real browser, not off the source: every one of the 164 cards it holds is drawn in the column the board puts it in, each heading counts what its own column drew, and the one dropped card is under Cancelled instead of hidden in Done. Your column is empty today and drawn oldest first, so the longest wait is always the top card. Both of those last two were made to fail on purpose before they were believed — a heading told to lie is named, and a column ordered the other way up goes red.

rows.title: Turning a job down does not start a new one
rows.note: What the reader objects to becomes more pieces of that same job, and the job goes back to the first column until someone picks one up. When they are all closed it returns to be read. Both directions are held by a check that touches no board.

content.label: The six columns
content.lead: Your words, and what each one means to the board.

rows: Any agent, by picking it up
Being worked, in its own copy of the project
In the game, waiting to be read by a second agent
The second agent, once it has read it
In the game and read, in your hands because no agent can judge it

blocks.text: Paused and blocked cards keep sitting in Todo with a small badge, as they do today. Nobody is on them, which is what Todo means.

rows.title: What being read means
rows.note: A second agent, one that did not write the change, opens the whole of it and judges it against what the card promised: does it do that, does it hold up, is anything wrong or missing. It either passes it or sends it back with its reasons, and those reasons start the next attempt. Nothing does this today — a job is closed by the agent that built it, and nothing anywhere checks that a second pair of eyes ever saw it.

content.label: Where a job shows when its pieces disagree
content.lead: Your rule, as the board now runs it.

rows: one being worked, the rest waiting
all of them closed and in the game

blocks.text: The column tells you where a job is stuck rather than how far its luckiest part got, and every card agrees with the list of pieces printed under it.

content.label: What changes for you
content.lead: Three things you cannot do today.

rows.title: See what is waiting on you
rows.note: Today a job that needs your eye is either closed by the agent that built it or sits in the first column looking unstarted. There are 157 finished cards on your board and not one of them carries your signature.

rows.title: Stop a card being ticked off behind you
rows.note: No agent can move a card out of your column. Not to finished, not back to the start. That is enforced, not agreed.

rows.title: Tell dropped work from delivered work
rows.note: Cancelled becomes its own column with the reason kept, instead of joining everything else under finished.

content.label: Four suggestions on top of your six
content.lead: You asked what would make it better. These are the four worth having.

items: A job declares at the start that you have to judge it, not at the end. The agent then owes you something to look at from its first day, instead of reconstructing one after the work is done — and it cannot quietly decide at the finish line that you do not need to see it.
Nothing reaches your column without the thing you are meant to look at. A picture, or a page like this one. A column full of cards you cannot act on is worse than no column.

Turning something down sends it back to the start carrying your words, and those words become the brief for the next attempt. The old job stays finished and honest; the new one starts from what you actually said.
Your column is shown oldest first with a count on it, so nothing sits there quietly for a week.

decisions.title: Cancelled is a finished card that says it was cancelled, not a new kind of open card
decisions.why: Anything waiting on a cancelled card would wait forever otherwise. It has to count as finished to the board, and read as dropped to you.

decisions.title: Manager Review is a real column on the board, not a tag on a card
decisions.why: A tag can be taken off by whoever put it on. A column can be held shut.

decisions.title: No agent can move a card out of your column in either direction
decisions.why: Sending it back would be as good as closing it. Only you decide it is finished, and only you decide it needs another go.

decisions.title: Agent Review means a job whose every piece is closed, waiting to be read
decisions.why: Your ruling of 13 August. It used to mean written-but-not-in-the-game, which is a landing rather than a review, and that is what made a job ask to be read after each of its steps.

decisions.title: Paused, blocked and pinned cards stay in Todo with a badge
decisions.why: Nobody is on them, which is what Todo means. Three more columns for three states you rarely act on would cost more than they tell you.

decisions.title: The board tests of itself are gone, and the cards they left behind with them
decisions.why: Your ruling. Forty-seven throwaway cards were sitting on your board pretending to be work, and the checks that made them are deleted. What holds the rules now is that every agent hits them on every board command.

decisions.title: Work goes into the game first and then waits in your column
decisions.why: Your answer to the first question this page asked. You judge it by playing the game, and nothing else queues behind it while it waits. Built and running.

decisions.title: Every job says when it opens whether you have to judge it
decisions.why: Your answer to the second question this page asked. It cannot be left blank and it cannot be added at the end to dodge a read. Built and running.

decisions.title: A card reads only the pieces directly under it, never the whole tree below
decisions.why: What put the fog job in the wrong column was a card four levels down. Reading one level is the only shape where a card and the list printed under it always agree. The cost: a folder of jobs reads as untouched while work runs inside one of them, because none of its own pieces has started. Say the word and it reads deeper.

decisions.title: A piece of work is never read on its own, and work not yet in the game is work still being done
decisions.why: Your ruling. A piece asking to be read after each small step is what emptied the word review of meaning; unlanded work is work still in hand, not work waiting on anybody.

decisions.title: Turning a job down adds pieces to that same job rather than opening a new one
decisions.why: Your ruling. A new job would leave the old one closed and honest-looking while the objection lived somewhere else; this way a job carries one list of what is left, and a reader's objection cannot be walked past by finishing around it.

decisions.title: A job sent back is read again once its new pieces close
decisions.why: Your words: back to Todo, then Agent Review, then your column. A second reading costs one reader per round and stops when a round finds nothing.

next.if_nothing: Your board runs the ruling and draws all six columns. Nothing here is waiting on you.
